title: Australia Sends Aid as Indian-Origin Australians Among 39 Missing in Nepal Floods
excerpt: Many of the missing Australians are Indian-origin pilgrims headed to Mount Kailash when the catastrophic flood struck the Nepal-Tibet border.
body:
• Australia announced a $5 million (AUD) aid package for Nepal and deployed additional consular staff as 39 Australians remain missing after the catastrophic Himalayan flood.
  • At least 15 of the missing Australians are Indian-Australians who were on a religious pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, including an 11-year-old boy, according to tour operator Himalayan Glacier.
  • Among those missing are Sandeep Mohapatra and his wife, an Australia-based couple originally from Odisha, India, whose family has heard nothing since August 24.
  • Indian spiritual leader Sadhguru said 77 pilgrims of various nationalities, along with three staff from his Isha Foundation, are among the missing from the flood zone.

Australia dispatched emergency aid and additional consular staff to Nepal on Friday as the number of missing Australians from this week's catastrophic Himalayan flood rose to 39 — many of them Indian-origin Australians on religious pilgrimages to some of Hinduism's holiest sites.

Foreign Minister Penny Wong announced the aid package in a joint statement with International Development Minister Anne Aly, warning that the scale of the disaster and the remoteness of the affected region present "immense challenges" for response and recovery.

Indian-Australians Among the Missing

Himalayan Glacier, a tourism agency operating in the region, confirmed that 15 of the missing Australians were part of a religious tour to Mount Kailash it had organized. All 15 were Indian-Australians, with the youngest an 11-year-old boy, the company's chief executive Sagar Pandey told Reuters.

"They were on a pilgrimage. They were planning to enter China's Tibet and go to Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar, which is one of the holiest landmarks on earth," Pandey said.

Pandey, who flew over the flood zone by helicopter to assess the situation, offered a grim assessment of the chances of finding survivors.

"There are no human-made things, no human settlement left. Everything is just flat. I believe that everybody is gone."

— Sagar Pandey, CEO, Himalayan Glacier

Families Desperate for News

Among the missing are Sandeep Mohapatra and his wife, an Australia-based couple originally from the eastern Indian state of Odisha. Their family has been unable to reach them since receiving a text message on August 24.

"We last spoke to them on August 23 and received a text message the next day. Since then, we have had no information about their whereabouts," Sandeep's cousin, Soumya Mohapatra, told Reuters. "We have lost hope after hearing about the scale of the destruction and the number of deaths."

Indian spiritual leader Sadhguru Jaggi Vasudev said 77 pilgrims of various nationalities, along with three staff members from his Isha Foundation, were among those missing. The group had completed the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage and was clearing immigration on the Chinese side of the border when all contact was lost.

Scale of the Crisis

The flash flood, triggered by a glacier collapse on Wednesday, has killed at least 359 people and left nearly 1,000 missing across Nepal and China's Tibet — more than half of them foreigners. Indians make up the largest group of missing foreigners, with 288 unaccounted for in Nepal and another 200 stranded in China.

Australia's aid funds will be split between the United Nations' World Food Programme and Australian NGOs. A crisis response specialist has already flown to Kathmandu, and a team of three humanitarian workers will deploy within 48 hours.

Wong said earlier Thursday that at least 34 Australians were part of "separate pilgrimage and tour groups" and that information from the disaster zone remained "very limited given the scale of disaster."

A Diaspora in Mourning

The disaster has struck at the heart of Indian diaspora communities across Australia, where Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimages are a deeply important spiritual tradition. August falls within the peak pilgrimage season, when weather conditions and access routes into Tibet are most favorable, drawing hundreds of devotees annually from India and its diaspora.

Communities across Australia have held vigils for those affected, while the Indian embassy in Kathmandu and authorities in several Indian states have set up helplines for families seeking information about their loved ones.
